title.rendered: Fuel cost must reflect crude prices

content.rendered:
THE Federal Government’s latest intervention in the fuel pricing debate is both timely and necessary. When the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Heineken Lokpobiri, and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission insist that petrol pump prices should reflect the recent decline in global crude oil prices, they are simply demanding fairness for consumers.

When geopolitical tensions between the United States, Israel and Iran pushed crude oil prices sharply higher, reaching $126 per barrel earlier this year, fuel prices in Nigeria rose immediately. Retail petrol prices surged from roughly N800–N900 per litre to as much as N1,350–N1,500 per litre in some locations.

Yet, now that tensions have eased, the Strait of Hormuz remains open, and Brent crude has fallen back toward the low-$70-per-barrel range; consumers are still paying around N1,140–N1,250 per litre. This should not be the case.

The FCCPC quickly flagged this disconnect. Executive Vice-Chairman/CEO Tunji Bello rightly noted that while “dealers often respond swiftly by hiking pump prices whenever crude prices rise, it is curious that it is taking forever for consumers to benefit significantly when crude prices fall. Competitive markets must work fairly in both directions”.

Significantly, this position mirrors concerns being expressed by United States President Donald Trump, who recently warned gasoline retailers of “problems” if they failed to lower prices in line with falling crude oil costs, describing excessive delays as potential price gouging.

The US Treasury Secretary has also echoed concerns over retailers failing to pass lower crude costs to consumers. The message from both Washington and Abuja is simply that deregulation is not a licence for exploitation.

However, the reality is more complicated than political statements suggest.

Fuel prices do not move in perfect lockstep with crude oil prices. Economists describe the phenomenon as “rockets and feathers” in reference to a situation where prices shoot up like rockets when costs rise but drift down like feathers when costs fall.

Mathematical modelling helps explain why.

Assuming that crude oil trades at $80 per barrel, the exchange rate is N1,500 per dollar, and local logistics, distribution, financing, regulatory and retail costs amount to about N350 per litre. Under those assumptions, the pump price could be around N1,293 per litre.

If crude oil falls from $80 to $70 per barrel while all other variables remain unchanged, the model suggests pump prices could decline by roughly N118 per litre.

By contrast, if the naira strengthens from N1,500 to N1,400 per dollar while crude remains unchanged, the reduction is closer to N63 per litre.

This shows that crude oil movements have a larger impact on fuel prices than comparable exchange-rate improvements because crude constitutes the largest cost component. Nevertheless, neither factor operates in isolation.

Nigeria’s fuel pricing structure contains several fixed and semi-fixed costs that do not automatically decline when crude prices fall.

Importers must still pay freight charges, marine insurance, ship-to-ship transfer fees, port charges, NMDPRA levies, depot fees, storage costs, bridging expenses, bank financing charges and retail margins. Local transportation costs remain heavily influenced by diesel prices and poor infrastructure.

Even local refining does not completely insulate Nigeria from international market realities. The Petroleum Industry Act links domestic crude supply obligations to international benchmarks.

For example, Dangote Refinery may eliminate some shipping and import costs, but it still purchases crude priced against global markets and remains exposed to exchange-rate risks.

Private refiners also have the option of exporting products if domestic prices become artificially unattractive.

These realities explain why pump prices may not fall as rapidly as crude prices. However, they do not justify the magnitude of the current gap.

The FCCPC is therefore correct to focus not on price fixing but on market behaviour. If marketers are genuinely selling older inventory purchased at higher costs, that can be verified.

If, however, companies are maintaining elevated prices long after replacement costs have fallen, regulators have every right to investigate potential anti-competitive conduct, stock hoarding, collusion or exploitative practices.

Regardless, the counterargument from marketers cannot be dismissed. Independent Petroleum Marketers Association of Nigeria officials insist that many operators are already suffering losses due to repeated price reductions by refiners.

IPMAN spokesman, Chinedu Ukadike, said: “We, the independent marketers, are losing money. We bought petrol at a particular rate a few days ago; on our way to our filling stations, there was a reduction.

“We have been struggling with the price. We have been struggling against financial losses. We are also struggling against stagnation due to low patronage of our products. Because those marketers who are purchasing now are purchasing at a lower price, and they are selling cheaper.”

Many marketers operate with expensive bank loans, fixed interest obligations and shrinking margins. They warn that any attempt to impose administrative price controls in a deregulated market would violate the spirit of the Petroleum Industry Act and could trigger widespread supply disruptions.

Ukadike has warned that “marketers will shut down if they try somehow to enforce price control. We are going to shut down our stations nationwide. You can’t be regulating a deregulated market. You can’t tell me how much to sell my product without trying to know how much I bought it.”

IPMAN is right that the government cannot simultaneously claim to have deregulated the downstream sector while surreptitiously reintroducing price controls. Such policy inconsistency would discourage investment and undermine confidence in the market.

But neither can deregulation become a cover for profiteering.

Deeper competition, not heavier regulation, appears to be the solution. More domestic refining capacity, easier access to imports, transparent publication of landing costs, stronger anti-cartel enforcement, efficient ports, lower logistics costs, and greater market transparency will naturally force prices downward.

Where competition is genuine, retailers that refuse to pass savings to consumers lose market share.

Ultimately, Nigerians deserve a fuel market that responds fairly to changing realities. If pump prices can rise within days when crude oil climbs, they should also decline within a reasonable timeframe when crude falls.

In an economy already burdened by inflation, weak purchasing power, and rising business costs, fuel prices affect virtually everything, from food, transport, and electricity costs to manufacturing and household budgets.

The government must resist the temptation of crude price controls, but it must be equally vigilant against market abuse. Deregulation should reward efficiency, not opportunism.
